text: To understand which biotech companies are finding the most success today, it is imperative that we consider the thoughts of those that are most involved in the industry. For example, a voice from a top life science and biotech VCs, OrbiMed Advisors, showed inclination towards neuroscience, obesity, and immunology, across modalities like RNA, small molecules, and proteins, while interest in previously hot areas, such as orphan drugs and gene therapy, has declined. Similarly, Arch Venture Partners has stated a desire to stay outside of crowded drug races, and bet instead on more niche science that is capable of large impact. Leaders from organizations like Deepmind have emphasized the importance of AI as a means of validation: A loop that links the dry and wet labs ensures the creation of a lasting science pipeline.

text: Neurotechnology: The brain is still one of the least-solved areas in medicine, and the rapid growth of AI is greatly accelerating how quickly we can understand its workings. With a better understanding of the brain, come technologies that better tackle neuro-based problems, from brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) to deep brain stimulation (DBS). The Alumni Ventures Deep Tech Fund itself has invested in Precision Neuroscience, for example, a BCI company unique for its Layer 7, ultra-thin technology that only solely attaches to, but does not penetrate, the brain, and allows bidirectional communication. We are excited to see further innovations in an area that so clearly benefits those with difficult neurological conditions.

text: Genetic Medicines & DNA: The entirety of the United States recently witnessed the widespread emergence of mRNA’s applications to medicine with the rise of mRNA-based COVID vaccines produced by Pfizer and Moderna. For context, mRNA technology is so revolutionary because it’s short-lived and does not integrate into the genome, making it an excellent and timely solution to a COVID, a spontaneous outbreak of a virus. Such technologies that use genetic medicines (any therapy involving nucleic acids, RNA or DNA, as their basis) will continue to have potential in other applications to medicine. A very relevant example: The creator of Moderna, Flagship Biosciences, unveiled Serif Biomedicines out of stealth in April of this year; with $50 million in funding, Serif investigates Modified DNA as a new modality of treating disease. For more information, see Decoding Bio’s interview with Serif’s CEO, Dr. Jake Rubens, here.

text: Horizontal Platforms: The picks-and-shovels layer. Rather than betting everything on one molecule, horizontal platforms sell the tools, infrastructure, data, or workflows that many drug developers need. They own a difficult bottleneck, such as discovery, delivery, lab automation, predictive biology, or bioprocessing, and make that bottleneck faster, more reliable, or more scalable for every customer.

text: But what exactly in the drug life cycle are the issues that prevent us from curing everything? Why do so many drugs fail? Why must so much time and money be invested into failed drug ventures?

text: To answer those questions, it’s important to look particularly at what is more or less indisputably the most critical stage of this life cycle: Clinical Trials. Before this stage, the efficacy of a drug on humans is never actually evaluated. Our preclinical science is simply not good enough to be a good predictor of clinical success.

text: And why does our preclinical science fail? NewLimit CEO Jacob Kimmel narrows the question down to two reasons: A) The drugs we engineer are engineered incorrectly and don’t hit their target molecule, or B) The drug does hit the target molecule, but the downstream effects fail to meet our expectations. Kimmel reasons that the latter is more abundant, but regardless, these two issues point us to three solutions: We need 1) a better way of hitting the same targets, 2) new targets, and 3) better modeling of downstream effects. This is a science problem.

text: This all said, the problem is definitely not a lack of simple therapeutics companies. More simple therapeutics will not magically surpass the scientific obstacles that already exist. AI is finally making its long-awaited march into the life sciences; it is imperative to direct this march into ventures that expand across the industry. A more efficient industry, built on a more intelligent science infrastructure, will discover more drugs more quickly and more accurately. Obviously the preclinical science stage is incredibly complex and disease/treatment-specific, but whether it is in-silico, in-vitro, or in-vivo, the companies that can prove themselves (not just in one particular vertical but with a large span of the industry) will succeed. They will provide the most value because that’s what biotech needs.
